solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Ducks again repelled predator

indicators.note: to repel is to drive something back, so the word is sent back the way it came, last letter first

parts.note: to duck is to dip, so ducks again = redips

explanation.surface: Some ducks have fended off an attacker a second time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ducks' looks like the birds, with the predator hunting them; it is the verb, dips, and 'again' adds RE.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain definition by kind: the spider traps and eats other creatures, which is all a predator does.

clue.text: Principal before Scrooge giving away shillings

indicators.note: to give something away is to part with it, so the miser loses the letter for shillings

parts.note: pre- = before
a Scrooge is a MISER; drop S for shillings

explanation.surface: A head teacher takes precedence over a mean man who is parting with his coins.
explanation.walkthrough: Scrooge is Dickens's miser, and S is the old abbreviation for a shilling, a pre-decimal British coin. A miser giving money away is the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words, as adjectives, mean first in rank or importance.

clue.text: Chest expander's broken rim had gap

indicators.note: something broken is in pieces, and the pieces of RIM HAD GAP are put back together in a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: A piece of gym equipment for stretching the chest has a cracked rim.
explanation.walkthrough: A chest expander is a sprung exercise device, which is what the surface wants you to see; here it is the muscle that expands the chest when you breathe in.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: the diaphragm muscle contracts to enlarge the chest cavity, so it literally expands the chest.

clue.text: Pro-Reform Conservative has quit, going from centre to extreme

indicators.note: someone who has quit has left, so the Conservative's letter leaves the word

parts.note: a radical wants reform
C = Conservative, the letter removed

explanation.surface: A reforming Tory has left the party and swung from the middle ground to the fringe.
explanation.walkthrough: The political surface makes 'from centre to extreme' read as a change of views; it is geometry, a line running from the middle outward.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: spokes and radii run from the hub out to the edge, which is what the adjective describes.

clue.text: Hide crop from antelope on small preserve

indicators.note: in an across clue, A on B puts A after B, as if resting on it

parts.note: s = small
jam is a fruit preserve
bok, South African for an antelope, as in springbok

explanation.surface: A crop of hides taken from an antelope kept on a small reserve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hide' and 'crop' look like farm produce, but together they name a whip made of hide: a crop is a riding whip.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by material and kind: the sjambok is a heavy South African whip of rhino or hippo hide.

clue.text: Second exit Spooner's passed in irritation

indicators.note: the Rev. William Spooner was famous for swapping the first sounds of words, so his version swaps them

parts.note: passed (away) = died; takes the S sound from its partner
sore = smarting, irritated; takes the D sound

explanation.surface: Someone left a second time, in a temper, as Spooner told it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second exit' reads like a second departure; it is a secondary way out of a building.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by function: a side door is a way out other than the main entrance, a second exit.

clue.text: Dominant peak that's lovely from below

parts.note: an alp is a mountain peak

indicators.note: read from below means read upward, and in a down clue that turns the letters round

parts.note: 'Ah!' is what you say at something lovely

explanation.surface: A towering mountain that looks its best when you gaze up at it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From below' fits the mountain view so well it reads as description; in a down clue it turns AH upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjective from animal behaviour: the alpha wolf or male leads the pack, so alpha has come to mean top-ranking.

clue.text: Incompetent musician who signals note has cracked

definitions.note: The answer is a noun; 'Incompetent' is read as a noun too, an incompetent person.

indicators.note: to crack something is to break into it, so the note breaks into the musician

parts.note: a bugler sounds calls in the army
n = note, as in footnote references

explanation.surface: A hopeless musician whose note cracks as he plays the signal.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'Incompetent musician' one phrase; the definition is only 'Incompetent', and the musician starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Noun for noun: someone who botches everything they try is an incompetent.

clue.text: Skirt that likely covers bottom up

indicators.note: the phrase covers the answer, holding it inside its letters
bottom up means starting from the bottom, and in a down clue that reads the letters upward

parts.note: thaT LIKely

explanation.surface: A skirt that probably hides someone's backside.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a joke about what a kilt conceals; 'bottom' is the backside and also the foot of the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by kind: the kilt is the knee-length pleated skirt of Scottish dress.

clue.text: Horse carrying protégé ran at the races

indicators.note: a horse carrying a rider holds it, so the horse's letters hold the protégé

parts.note: a steed is a horse
a ward is someone under a guardian's protection

explanation.surface: A racehorse carrying its young rider ran in a race meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ran at the races' looks like a horse running; it means organised the meeting, as the stewards do.
explanation.definitionFit: A specialist sense: race stewards run and police a meeting, so to steward a race meeting is to run it.

clue.text: Lower class eagle golf coach picked up

indicators.note: something picked up is lifted, so in a down clue the letters read upward

parts.note: the erne is the sea eagle
G is golf in the radio alphabet
a coach is a bus

explanation.surface: A golf coach of humble origins, noticed for scoring an eagle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lower class' sounds social; it is a category below another. 'Eagle' and 'golf' together look like a golf score.
explanation.definitionFit: A taxonomic sense: in classifying books, films or music, a subgenre sits one level below a genre.

clue.text: Quiz show contestants perhaps left in flat coming last

indicators.note: whatever comes last arrives at the end

parts.note: a plane is a flat surface
l = left; take it out of PLANE and put it at the end

explanation.surface: Quiz contestants left in a flat after finishing last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coming last' reads as the contestants' bad result, which is why the letter move is easy to miss. 'Perhaps' marks quiz contestants as one kind of panel.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: many quiz shows seat their contestants as a panel.

clue.text: First thing honest outlaw admits, at great cost

parts.note: to outlaw something is to ban it
right = morally proper, upright
paid dearly = at great cost

explanation.surface: The first thing an honest robber confesses is that it cost him a lot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outlaw' is a noun in the surface and the verb, to ban, in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Two idioms for the same time: 'first thing' and 'bright and early' both mean at the start of the day.

clue.text: Have good aim? Poor, I suppose

parts.note: mean = poor, shabby
'Well…' is a grudging 'I suppose'

explanation.surface: An archer asks if they shoot straight, and gets a lukewarm reply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aim' reads as marksmanship; it is intention. The question mark flags that sideways use.
explanation.definitionFit: A playful sense: aim can mean intention, and good intentions are what meaning well is.

clue.text: Are blunders by Washington Times what may prejudice hearing?

indicators.note: a word that blunders stumbles about, so its letters end up out of order
one thing by another sits beside it, so the pieces are placed side by side

parts.note: anagram of ARE
WA is the postal code for Washington State
x = times, the multiplication sign

explanation.surface: Does a newspaper's mistakes bias a court hearing?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Washington Times' is a real newspaper and 'prejudice hearing' is legal language; the hearing is the sense of hearing.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: a build-up of wax in the ears can impair, or prejudice, how well you hear.

clue.text: 1,000 miles crossed by railroad traffic

indicators.note: a place crossed by a railway has the line running through it

parts.note: to railroad someone is to coerce them
M is the Roman numeral for 1,000
m = miles

explanation.surface: A thousand miles of track carrying rail traffic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Railroad' belongs with 'traffic' in the surface; in the wordplay it is the verb, to force.
explanation.definitionFit: An older sense of traffic: trade or dealing, as in drug traffic, which is commerce.

clue.text: Precisely circling globe after second launch, say

indicators.note: to circle something is to go round it

parts.note: a mo is a moment, a second

indicators.note: one thing after another follows it

parts.note: to a T = precisely
an orb is a globe

explanation.surface: A spacecraft orbiting the earth with exact timing after its second launch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Launch' reads as a rocket going up; a launch is also a boat. 'Say' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a launch is one kind of powered boat, hence 'say'.

clue.text: Doctor cycles around area and runs not at all

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters are altered into a new order
CYCLES goes around the other letters before they are all mixed

parts.note: anagram fodder
a = area
r = runs, in cricket scoring

explanation.surface: A GP who cycles round the neighbourhood and never goes running.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like the person cycling; it is the command to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: 'I scarcely knew him' is close to 'not at all', and Chambers allows the stronger sense.

clue.text: Bats acquire new means to fight chill

parts.note: to rearm is to get new weapons
to ice is to chill

explanation.surface: Bats are gathering fresh weapons against the cold.
explanation.walkthrough: The archaic word is worth learning, because the charade is easy once you know it exists.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic word: rearmouse, or reremouse, is an old English name for a bat.

clue.text: Having no restraint in back of Fiesta, belt attached

definitions.note: The answer is a noun, a lack of restraint; the definition reads as a phrase describing that state, as in 'with abandon'.

parts.note: last letter of Fiesta
a band is a belt, a strip
on = attached, as in 'the lid is on'

explanation.surface: Someone lolling unbelted in the back seat of a Ford Fiesta.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fiesta is a Ford car, so 'back of Fiesta' and 'belt' suggest a seatbelt left undone.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: to dance with abandon is to dance with no restraint at all.

clue.text: Useful bit of information, part of prescription for many

parts.note: a stat, a statistic, is a useful fact
the first two letters of information

explanation.surface: A handy fact that forms part of the advice given to many people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prescription' reads as advice in general; it is a doctor's prescription, and statins are among the most widely prescribed drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: cholesterol-lowering statins are taken daily by millions, so they appear on many prescriptions.

clue.text: These all downed on strike?

parts.note: reads as workers who have all downed tools; in fact things knocked over
reads as industrial action; in fact the bowling term for felling everything with one ball

explanation.surface: Workers who all put down tools when a strike is called.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Downed' and 'strike' suggest industrial action; a strike in bowling fells all ten pins at once.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic definition: in tenpin bowling a strike knocks down every pin with the first ball.

clue.text: Taking pen, draw over diamonds with something similar

parts.note: to ink in a pencil drawing is to go over it in pen
D = diamonds, the card suit

explanation.surface: An artist picks up a pen and traces over a diamond pattern.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draw over' looks like sketching on top of something; inking in is exactly that, done with a pen.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: repaying a favour or insult in kind means returning the same sort of thing.

clue.text: One with rind — anagram rearranges it

definitions.text: One with rind — anagram rearranges it

indicators.note: to rearrange is to put things in a new order, here the letters

parts.note: anagram fodder
anagram fodder
the word itself is fodder too

explanation.surface: A clue that announces its own trick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Anagram' looks like a signal but is itself fodder, and 'One with rind' does double duty as letters and as a description of the fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: a citrus fruit with rind, whose name is an anagram of 'one rind anagram'.

clue.text: Kentish boy perhaps raised in Yorkshire countryside

indicators.note: something raised is lifted up, so in a down clue the letters read upward

parts.note: Kent is in the south-east of England
a lad is a boy; 'perhaps' because SE LAD is just one example of a Kentish boy

explanation.surface: A boy from Kent brought up in rural Yorkshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Kent is a county in south-east England, hence SE. 'Raised' reads as brought up, the childhood of the Kentish boy.
explanation.definitionFit: A proper name: the Yorkshire Dales are the valleys and uplands of northern England's largest county.

clue.text: Second home — one affecting minister's judgement?

parts.note: s = second
a pad is slang for one's home

explanation.surface: An MP's second home is the thing that clouds his judgement.
explanation.walkthrough: A SpAd is a special adviser, a political appointee who advises a British government minister. 'Second home' recalls MPs' expenses scandals.
explanation.definitionFit: A description by role: advisers exist to shape a minister's decisions; the question mark admits the gentle dig.

clue.text: Tennis game old man was winning on return

parts.note: one's old man is one's father, pa

indicators.note: something on its return comes back the way it went, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: led = was ahead

explanation.surface: Dad was winning a tennis match on his return of serve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On return' fits tennis so well it reads as the return of serve; it reverses LED.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by kind: padel is a racket game related to tennis, played in a small walled court.

clue.text: Leaderless Jedi pilot catches Oscar making script changes

indicators.note: a word without its leader has lost its first letter

parts.note: JEDI without its J

indicators.note: to catch something is to hold it

parts.note: a pilot scheme is a trial
O is Oscar in the radio alphabet

explanation.surface: A Star Wars pilot scoops an Oscar for his script.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pilot' and 'Jedi' point to spaceships; the pilot is a trial run, like a pilot episode.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjective by activity: editorial work is the correcting and reshaping of a text.

clue.text: Line extended by ruler?

parts.note: reads as a drawn line lengthened; in fact a family line continued
reads as a straight-edge; in fact a monarch, each one adding a generation

explanation.surface: Drawing a longer line with a ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: The ruler is a straight-edge in the surface; it is a monarch, and the line is a royal family's succession.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic definition: each new king or queen of the same house lengthens the family's line of rulers.

clue.text: Silly person with looks bored by books

indicators.note: something bored by a drill has a hole through it, so the books sit inside

parts.note: a dish is an attractive person
OT = Old Testament, a set of books

explanation.surface: A fool who is good-looking gets bored by reading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silly person' reads as one unit, but the definition is just 'Silly'; 'person with looks' is the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A dialect word: dotish, from dote, means foolish.
